explanations.39: T is the line number where the truncate comment appears, E is the total line count, and BODY is how many lines of actual content follow the truncate — think of it as the 'real article' length.
explanations.42: If QuickJump appears right after the truncate anchor, pretend it isn't there for measurement purposes — move your starting point past it so navigation scaffolding doesn't artificially inflate how far down the proof appears.
explanations.64: If an article has zero proof (no output shown, no images, no visible results), the time-to-value is 100% — meaning the reader never actually sees the payoff.
explanations.68: These percentages (15%, 30%) measure how far down the page a reader has to scroll before they see actual proof the thing works — lower is better because they see results sooner.
explanations.69: A 'red flag' here means it fails automatically — if you have to install something before the article shows you what it does, that's a problem worth noting.
explanations.87: This awk command counts the word count per section by finding each heading and tallying words between them — it's a quick way to spot if one section is bloated compared to others.
